item.title: When Kindness Meets Hate: What Parents Can Teach Children
item.description:
Parenting

When Kindness Meets Hate: What Parents Can Teach Children

Parents can build emotional intelligence amid a culture of division.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Fear, anger, and pain are real, but they don’t justify hatred or dehumanization.
  • Strong disagreement and accountability can coexist with dignity and respect.
  • Kids need to learn to identify emotions, question assumptions, and consider the impact of their actions.

Co-authored with Bridget Harris

A few months ago, Sesame Street posted a simple message for Jewish American Heritage Month. The spirit of the post was unmistakable: celebration, inclusion, belonging.

Yet the comment section rapidly filled with vile antisemitism before it was turned off. A post from Sesame Street—created to help children grow “smarter, stronger, and kinder”—became a target for contempt.

Kindness was met with hate.

For parents, educators, and all of us who care about young people, this is not simply a social media story. It is a developmental story. Children are watching how adults respond when fear rises, anger hardens, people disagree, groups are blamed, and cruelty is excused as humor, politics, or “just how people talk online.”

The Jewish High Holy Days are a time to gather and reflect. They’re also an apt moment to ponder what feeds “isms” like antisemitism—and, critically, what we can teach children and teens so they do not inherit the dangerous spiral of “You hate me, I hate you; you hurt me, I hurt you back.”

Feelings Are Information, Not Instructions

Antisemitism, like other forms of group hatred, often begins with a story—a story built out of fear, anger, grievance, humiliation, confusion, or pain. Those feelings may be real. But they become dangerous when they are turned into false conclusions: I feel afraid, so you must be a threat. I feel powerless, so your group must be to blame. I feel angry, so cruelty is justified.

This is why one of the first lessons we can teach children is also one of the most important lessons of emotional intelligence: Feelings are information, but they are not instructions.

Fear deserves attention, but it does not prove another group is dangerous. Anger can alert us to injustice, but it does not give us permission to dehumanize. Pain may explain why someone wants to lash out, but it does not excuse turning a whole group into a target.

Hatred can be seductive to young people because it offers a false kind of strength: certainty instead of confusion, belonging instead of loneliness, superiority over shame.

Telling children simply “don’t hate” is not enough. We need to help them work with the emotions that make hatred so contagious: fear, anger, shame, belonging, and the wish to be accepted by the group. We can help them ask: What am I feeling? What story am I telling myself? What do I know, and what am I assuming? Who might be harmed if I share this? What would my best self do next?

Disagreement Should Not Become Dehumanization

Antisemitism, as with many forms of prejudice and othering, thrives when one group of people is no longer seen as neighbors, classmates, teachers, doctors, artists, children, grandparents, and friends, but rather as a category, a symbol, a suspicion, a conspiracy, or a threat. It thrives when curiosity collapses, and when old stereotypes travel at the speed of a comment thread.

Parents can help their children make an essential distinction: Disagreement is not hatred. But a permission structure is created when people mock others and are rewarded for it, when cruelty is dismissed as “just a joke,” or when group hatred is excused because “everyone is angry.” Young people notice all of this.

When that cruelty is practiced by public leaders, online influencers, celebrities, or adults at our own dinner tables, parents have to become even more intentional about what they model at home.

Parents can say, clearly and calmly: “In our family, anger is allowed; dehumanizing is not.” “That person may be powerful, but that does not make the behavior right.” “We can disagree strongly without humiliating.” These sentences matter because they build a counter-permission structure.

This is how families become small schools of moral resistance: by helping children see the culture clearly and practice a different way of being inside it.

Empathy Stops Us From Mirroring Harm

Empathy is central here, but empathy is often misunderstood. Empathy does not mean agreeing with everyone, excusing harm, or avoiding accountability. Empathy means remembering that another person has an inner life as vivid and vulnerable as our own.

Empathy develops through emotional intelligence skills that help children pause, identify what they are feeling, and ask what someone else may be feeling, needing, or carrying. It helps them resist absorbing a stereotype or repeating a cruel joke and instead recognize the humanity of a Jewish or Muslim classmate, Christian or Hindu neighbor, Black or Indian teacher, or differently abled friend.

Children need to learn that when someone hates them, the answer is not to become hateful in return. The answer is to protect oneself, seek help, set boundaries, tell the truth, and refuse to become a mirror of the harm.

We Need to Lead With Our "Best Self"

Finally, we can help young people imagine and practice their Best Self. Our Best Self is who we want to be, and who we want others to see, when it matters most: brave, fair, curious, compassionate, and strong enough not to join in cruelty. It is the self that pauses before posting, asks before assuming, reaches for dignity instead of contempt, and understands that belonging is not a scarce resource.

Sesame Street had to turn off comments because kindness toward Jewish Americans invited hate. That painful teachable moment shows us what happens when empathy is not cultivated.

Our children are watching.

They are learning from what we condemn, what we excuse, what we laugh at, what we interrupt, and what we repair. The task before parents is not to raise children who never feel anger, fear, or hurt. The task is to raise children who know what to do with those feelings—children who can tell the truth without hatred, stand up without dehumanizing, and refuse to keep the old spiral going.

That is how we begin to build a different inheritance.

item.title: Responding Skillfully to Uncertainty
item.description:
Anxiety

Responding Skillfully to Uncertainty

Learn to take values-based action, even when you don’t know what comes next.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Uncertainty is a natural part of life, and it is associated with mental health challenges.
  • Cultivating curiosity and spaciousness can help buffer these challenges.
  • Choosing intentional, values-aligned actions amid uncertainty can bring meaning.
Source: Josh Bartok/ Used with permission

By Lizabeth Roemer, Ph.D., and Josh Bartok, M.S.

In times such as these, life may seem more uncertain than ever—but meeting uncertainty has always been part of our lives. Whenever we try new things, we are putting ourselves into uncertain contexts that could contain social threats, disappointments, or hurt. When our routines change (due to a new school year, transition at work, move, birth, death, or break-up), we face uncertainty about how we will adapt and what the near or far future might look like. And of course, right now, our sociopolitical context is filled with sources of uncertainty—the impact of climate change, high-stakes political upheavals, economic challenges, and other injustices and sources of real and potential harm.

Psychological research indicates that uncertainty is related to mental health challenges, including anxiety and depression. It is human to experience fear and distress, and it is human to have a desire to constrict or avoid when faced with uncertain threats or challenges. Often uncertain contexts lead to habits of worry—trying to plan, predict, or avoid threat by going through possibilities in our mind and choosing actions that will, we superstitiously imagine, somehow guarantee our safety. Planning is helpful in many cases, of course, but when there isn’t a problem we can solve with planning, this becomes a habit of worry that can leave us feeling more anxious, limiting and restricting our lives.

The following three-part approach can help you to face the inevitable uncertainty you encounter in ways that expand, rather than constrict, your life.

Notice when you encounter uncertainty

The first step in making meaningful, intentional changes in your habitual reactions is noticing the opportunities for this change. Consider how your mind and body react to uncertainty. You may notice a pit in your stomach, a tension across your shoulders, your mind getting busy and coming up with multiple potential outcomes to a given situation, or a sense of shutting down and wanting to avoid engaging in certain situations. Identifying how uncertainty shows up in your body and mind will help you recognize moments when you are having a strong reaction to uncertainty, so that you can practice a new response. And then, once you’ve noticed this, you can simply name it and acknowledge its presence, “Ah yes, uncertainty is here, and reactions are arising.”

Cultivate curiosity instead of seeking certainty

Having noticed and named the pull of habitual reactions to uncertainty, you can look more deeply at them. Notice, for instance, reactions that involve seeking certainty (avoiding, worrying, frantically trying to find a way to counter uncertainty), and then invite yourself to practice being curious about the context you find yourself in. When your mind tells you that you are definitely in danger, ask yourself whether there are any other possibilities or realities. When you feel a rush of anxious arousal, notice what that feels like in your body, rather than judging it or assuming your anxious thoughts are “true.” Do you notice anything beyond, behind, or amid the anxiety? You may find it helpful to intentionally cultivate spacious awareness with curiosity. Are there other thoughts arising, or other sensations you can notice in your body? Does the intensity of your bodily sensations vary over time?

Anything you do to disrupt the habitual constriction tied to uncertainty will enhance your ability to find ways to thrive even when you don’t know what may come next. Changing habits takes practice—keep applying strategy again and again, with compassion for yourself for your natural, human reactions.

Choose meaningful actions amid uncertainty

Although you may naturally have an impulse to constrain, avoid, or control in the face of uncertainty, you can instead choose to act according to what matters to you, what actions are in line with being, in this moment, the person you mean to be. Notice that you are constricting or worrying in response to uncertainty; practice loosening this habitual reaction by cultivating curiosity and acknowledging that not knowing truly is a whole and legitimate response to the reality that you do not know (which is to say, don’t let the reality of not knowing turn into a fictional certainty that you do know that things are as certainly dangerous as your anxious arousal is telling you). From this place of pausing in curiosity, you can consider how you would like to act in this moment.

While we often cannot control the external events that elicit fears and uncertainty, we do have control and agency over how we act in response to them. In any moment, you can choose to take one single step toward the person you’d like to be. And the beauty of this is that you can do it even while you feel anxious and uncertain, even while you feel scared. Values-based actions won’t eliminate uncertainty or remove anxiety, but they will often add a sense of purpose, meaning, or satisfaction, which can enhance your well-being and reduce the negative impact of uncertainty and anxiety.

Josh Bartok is a contemplative photographer and life coach, and the author of two children’s books.

item.title: Taking a Training Mindset to Climb Past Every Obstacle
item.description:
Sport and Competition

Taking a Training Mindset to Climb Past Every Obstacle

Elite climber Sam MacIlwaine offers insight in a special Batman Day interview.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Training is at the core of achievement.
  • People can train to withstand great hardship in order to achieve their goals.
  • Fictional characters like Batman can provide inspiration to help shape a resilient mindset.

The inmates chant, and a cauldron of bats roils around him as Bruce Wayne ditches the rope and finally climbs out of the pit where Bane imprisoned him in The Dark Knight Rises. It's a triumph heralding a return to Gotham City and imminent reckoning, leveraging training with an iron will.

While it works on screen, it's not exactly the way Sam MacIlwaine, elite climber, adventurer, and associate editor at Climbing magazine, would play it.

Fear of Failing and Falling

EPZ: You recently completed an epic “urban climb” at Autobahn in Germany. How does, or maybe doesn't, fear play a role in preparing for and then doing a challenging climb?

Sam MacIlwaine: Fear is definitely part of climbing. There's the basic fear of heights, which everyone has. I thought I didn't, but when I climbed El Capitan at about 2,000 feet, it kicked in, and I started thinking, I can't look down; I have to restrict myself and just stare at the wall. But there's a difference between fear and risk. In climbing, risk is very much acknowledged as something that is objective and something you can choose to take or not. Fear is a tool to alert you to risk, but it also can hold you back.

Sam Macilwaine traversing the Autobahn bridge.
Source: Dimitiri Roggon /Used with permission

EPZ: I really like this idea of fear as a kind of early warning signal to acknowledge and use.

SM: Climbers have to work really hard to align their sense of comfort with their objective reality. Sometimes accepting that risk of big falls is necessary in order to send something that is truly very difficult, where you might not feel 100 percent secure, but you're going to do anyway.

Training, Training, Rinse, Repeat; It's All Mental

EPZ: What is your mental state when you are climbing?

SM: With Autobahn, that kind of climb is very hard but extremely predictable. There's nothing that you need to do that's different, and the weight actually gets easier. It becomes all about pain management and tolerance. But you can train for that.

article continues after advertisement

EPZ: You have written about your climbs that "it’s all mental." Does this transfer into other aspects of your life?

Sam crossing the Autobahn.
Source: Dimitir Roggon / Used with permission.

SM: Yes. When I first started climbing, I wanted some sort of reassurance that what I'd done in the past meant I was going to be successful in the future. Now, after all this training and talking with professional athletes as a journalist, I don't believe that anything in your past guarantees future success. You just need to believe in yourself and decide, “I'm going to make this happen."

EPZ: That resonates because it fits with Batman taking a long time training to get somewhere and my own life in martial arts. The point is the process and purpose of training.

SM: Pursuing these big objectives is kind of a paradox: Sometimes you can't send the route until you let go of the need to do that. I am comfortable being the kind of person who's known as the girl who tried it for forever and never gave up.

About that scene in The Dark Knight Rises...

EPZ: You wrote “didn’t training mean training to go for it,” and it really resonated with me as a core principle of Batman and life in general.

SM: You need to be in the moment, with overwhelming desire, and it needs to be unacceptable for you to fall; to push yourself at that 98, 99 level of pain for so long, staying and staying and not quitting. It reminds me of The Dark Knight Rises, when Batman's trying to get out of that prison.

EPZ: What’s your take?

Sam Macilwaine under the Autobahn.
Source: Dimitiri Roggon /Used with permission

SM: For him to succeed on his last jump attempt, he takes out the rope, but I don't think that is necessary. I'm more likely to push harder and jump farther if I know I'm going to be protected, but I understand the mental effect of thinking I'm gonna die, and a reserve of strength comes in. Near the end of Autobahn, when I was over the concrete part, I knew I could not fall; I felt that. When you're climbing, and on the edge of pain and death, it kind of relaxes you a little bit, because you're not struggling to be like, should I… can I fall? Should I let go?

article continues after advertisement

EPZ: That's where all of your preparation and training comes together—riffing on a line from Batman Begins, it’s not just training but having the "will to act"?

SM: Yes, training is nothing compared to the will to act. I think that's so relevant to many things, especially climbing.

EPZ: How do you think Batman and characters like that can fit in with motivation and inspiration?

SM: As an athlete trying to reach their limit, it's important to surround yourself with stories like superheroes. I read a lot of fantasy books, watch a lot of fantasy television, and am very specific about the kind of characters that I align myself with. If a character is passive and not smart, or not up against something that feels impossible, then it's just not the thing for me to read. I need to fill my mind with the attitude of someone charging headfirst into a situation that they might not succeed in, but doing it because it aligns with their values; they know who they are and how they need to respond. I want to have the strength or background of Batman, that courage. You do need to have that, especially if you're doing something that's scary, you know?

Sam after completing her mission.
Source: Dimitiri Roggon / Used with permission

After my interview with Sam, I continued thinking more about Batman's mythology and how fictional characters can inspire. About how my mom’s interest in comics brought me to Batman, then into martial arts and to science. We all have the capacity to do more. We just have to have the determination to let go of the rope and put our bit of Batman to good use.

*Interview conducted Thursday, September 10, 2026.

© E. Paul Zehr (2026)

item.title: Is Most A Priori Philosophy a Waste?
item.description:
Philosophy

Is Most A Priori Philosophy a Waste?

A bold interview explains why pure philosophy must embrace empirical science.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Theoretical philosophy that ignores empirical data fails to advance human knowledge.
  • Conceptual and empirical inquiry overlap; philosophy requires evidence to yield meaningful truth.
  • Merging philosophical analysis with scientific research creates a unified, evidence-based discipline.
Is most a priori philosophy a waste of time and space?
Source: Image created with Chat-GPT

In an interview for the Undergraduate Philosophy Journal of Australasia in 2022, Australian philosopher Kim Sterelny (my wife's PhD advisor and one of my PhD supervisors) was asked about his most controversial view. His answer:

"Probably the view that most a priori philosophy is a complete waste of time. Take all the metaphysical stuff on the nature of grounding—that is just killing trees for no good reason. Complete and utter f*****g waste of time. A good deal of a priori philosophy is like that, and in my view, a waste of space. Does that do for controversial?"

Is Sterelny right?

Yes.

Nevertheless, his comments will certainly strike some readers as quite radical. So let’s look at how he justifies his position in response to the interviewer:

What do you think separates philosophy and the sciences? Do you think that there are questions currently considered to be in the realm of philosophy that in fact need to be addressed by people from other disciplines as well?

Well, I’m a radical on this. I don’t think there’s a sharp distinction between philosophy and science.

Now the title of my blog on Psychology Today is "Science and Philosophy," but as it happens, I agree with Sterelny. Philosophers of science since in the tradition of Quine realized that the common division drawn between the two rests on a mistake.

Sterelny continues:

There’s a kind of standard, conventional view that there are conceptual structures we can investigate a priori, and there’s the nature of the world we can investigate empirically. According to this view, the job of philosophy is to investigate conceptual structures in an a priori way, and the job of the sciences is to investigate the world and say what does or does not satisfy the conceptual structures that are identified in philosophy. I’m very sceptical about this division of labour. I don’t think there’s a sharp dividing line at any point that separates the wholly empirical questions from the wholly conceptual questions.

Exactly. Almost any significant philosophical question involves empirical data to some extent. And science itself isn't reducible to a simplistic vision of the experimental method without any attention to concepts. If we draw that distinction between science and philosophy, scientists are engaged in philosophy all the time.

Take the example of biology that Sterelny mentions:

If you read philosophical or biological literature, there’s no clean segmentation of conceptual issues, like ‘What is the nature of a gene?’ and empirical questions, like ‘What counts as a species?’ Because what you’re trying to come up with is for the purposes of trying to understand the biological world. The question, ‘What’s our most useful concept of species?’ can’t be answered without thinking about what the biological world is and what the phenomenon is that we need to explain. There isn’t a question that you can ask and answer independently of thinking about what your environment is. So I don’t think of there being any realm of ‘wholly philosophical questions’ or ‘wholly empirical questions.’ For me, the question of what knowledge is has an empirical dimension—questions about the nature of mind, cognition, consciousness, and so on. So, I think philosophical questions should be answered with an eye to the empirical world. I think all important questions have an empirical dimension.

Most professional philosophers who engage in a priori philosophy don’t just waste their time, space (and trees); they produce pseudo-philosophy, no longer meeting academic standards, damaging the reputation of philosophy, and harming our collective pursuit of objective truths. Philosophy must be deeply intertwined with science, since there is no independent foundation from which we could make philosophical judgements or judge science itself.

To use a metaphor by Otto Neurath, it's better to think of our attempts to build knowledge, science and philosophy, as something like a large ship that we are improving at sea. Science and philosophy are best served by merging into a unified field. Or as it used to be called: natural philosophy.

item.title: Do Left-Handers Have More Sleep Problems Than Right-Handers?
item.description:
Sleep

Do Left-Handers Have More Sleep Problems Than Right-Handers?

A study investigated whether handedness is linked to sleep problems.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Historically, it has been unclear whether left-handedness is linked to sleeping problems.
  • A study in more than 1,700 volunteers investigated the link between handedness and sleep.
  • Research shows that left-handers wake up more often at night and are sleepier during the day.

Most people are right-handed, but about 10.6 percent are left-handed. Interestingly, there have been reports that handedness may influence sleep quality, but they have been inconsistent. Some small studies suggest left-handers may have better sleep, while others suggest they wake more often at night. However, these studies only tested a few volunteers and relied on self-reports, not accurate scientific measurements. Thus, for a long time, it has been unclear whether handedness affects sleep quality.

A new study design

A 2022 study in Nature and Science of Sleep investigated the effects of handedness on sleep problems at night and sleepiness during the day (Taubert et al., 2022). The study, titled “Non-Right Handedness Is Associated With More Time Awake After Sleep Onset and Higher Daytime Sleepiness Than Right Handedness: Objective (Actigraphic) and Subjective Data from a Large Community Sample,” improved many of the weak spots of previous studies on handedness and sleep.

First, the scientists tested many volunteers over five consecutive nights. More than 1,700 volunteers aged between 18 and 80 participated in the study.

Second, the scientists used more accurate measurement methods than previous studies. So-called actigraphy was used to gather scientifically accurate and objective sleep data. An actigraph is a small device that looks similar to a watch and is worn on the wrist. It measures motor activity in the wearer, as well as skin temperature, temperature changes, and sweating. Since sleep phases differ in movements and other parameters, actigraphy can be used to measure different sleep phases, like REM sleep and non-REM sleep. The actigraph can measure the total sleep time, but also how many times someone wakes up at night and how efficiently they sleep. In addition, the volunteers in the study also filled out the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, a self-report questionnaire on subjective sleep quality.

Last but not least, volunteers filled out the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory, a commonly used questionnaire to determine handedness. This not only allowed the scientists to determine whether a volunteer was left-handed or right-handed, but also how strongly they were left- or right-handed.

Key findings

Overall, 91 percent of the volunteers in the study were right-handed, 4.8 percent were left-handed, and 4.2 percent were mixed-handed. For objective sleep parameters, it was found that the time spent awake after sleep onset was linked to handedness. The more left-handed someone was, the more time they spent getting awake again after falling asleep. Thus, the objective sleep quality of left-handers was lower than that of right-handers. In older men and women, the subjective sleep quality was also worse in left-handers compared to right-handers. Moreover, the more left-handed someone was, the more they showed sleepiness during the day.

The takeaway

To answer the question from the title of this post: Yes, non-right-handed people indeed have more sleep problems than right-handers, and they are also more often sleepy during the day. So if you are a lefty, it is especially important to take precautions for good sleep quality, like avoiding alcohol and reducing screen time before sleep.

item.title: A Book Review of Nora Bateson’s “Belly"
item.description:
Education

A Book Review of Nora Bateson’s “Belly"

How one’s kitchen interfaces with every aspect of our lives.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Nora Bateson’s "Belly" uses her kitchen to illustrate ecological and systemic interdependency.
  • Context shifts are key; recipes aren’t meals—life's complexity can't fit inside models or manuals.
  • Mutual learning emerges by "dancing in the kitchen," not following content or linear cause and effect.

“Between us is the genesis of ability to perceive and respond to the complexity of this time” -Nora Bateson

In the mid-'70s, my advisor at Columbia University, Paul Byers, gave me a copy of Steps to an Ecology of Mind by Gregory Bateson. It was my awakening to what I call a "first-order change": recognizing that something needs to be corrected. In my case, it was shifting from the narrow cause-and-effect perception shaped by my upbringing to realizing the world made better sense and offered more possibilities through the lens of ecological thinking.

Years later, I experienced Nora Bateson and her Warm Data process, a way to understand the patterns of our interdependence through mutual learning with others. It helped me access many new levels, or orders, of change and the difference between how we think and how nature works.

Source: Nora Bateson

In Nora's new and extremely relevant book to today's problems and polarization, Belly, she offers solutions through the ecology of communication and systems thinking that emanates from her kitchen.

It takes us on a journey that is an expression of our interdependency in what she describes as “the entire biosphere is ingesting and transforming everything into something to be ingested." This reminds me of Pablo Neruda's poem, “We go where nothing is expected and find everything waiting there.” This is systems thinking, which pushes us beyond the assumed certainty of quick-fix solutions and to look at life from a wider lens.

Nora's ever-evolving insights are shaped in part by her grandfather, biologist William Bateson, and her father, anthropologist Gregory Bateson, an excellent example of intergenerational learning. She supports this by describing, in warm human narratives, how dinner at her kitchen table is an excellent forum for creating new possibilities for living. She believes this influences our evolution as a species. Through this magical book of poems, narratives, and art, we can understand how much we have to "learn about learning."

She encourages us to thread conversations through contexts that have been separated and moved toward fragmentation, such as schooling, business, government, and media. This transcontextual communication should include people of all ages and backgrounds. This is the reality and coherence of our interdependency. She reminds us with many examples that "you can't take the grapes out of the wine." We are part of, and regardless of our differences, always interfacing with, our forests, oceans, religions, media, meadows, etc., which are always changing and seeking balance with each other and ourselves.

Nora asks the question, “How does change happen?" This is a difficult conversation, so bear with me, as Nora shows how the ecology of communication can manifest in her own kitchen or yours. She believes that “the recipe is not the meal,” and emphasizes the importance of learning that situations are contexts that shift, grow, and change.

She explains how, for instance, a refrigerator with its purpose and the origin of its contents relates to “an entire cosmos within which to discover being alive together," such as the origin of your vegetables, their seeds, the farmer who planted them, the people who got them to the market, and so on.

Nora narrates how, within systems thinking or ecology, the importance of having a beginner's mind in this process is that a “response to a situation is always limited by what possibilities are perceived." This matters because different contexts, i.e., your kitchen or mine, do not fit rigid models; we all differ yet share commonalities and needs. This pressure for uniformity creates misunderstanding and a lack of context that is deadly to all organisms and their environments. We and all living entities can respond to our surroundings in many ways; for example, trees share information about their growth and dangers.

Nora advocates fostering this way of understanding and change, what she calls a “ready-ing” of mutual learning that informs and blends all organisms' histories. Her descriptions of the different contexts in her own kitchen bring these thoughts into focus. She wants her kitchen to be “homey with smells of recently cooked meals." The complexity of life lies in the contextual possibilities that emerge in her kitchen, which she vividly brings to life in this book. This is poetically described as going beyond the linear cause-and-effect that stifles mutuality. She advocates breaking the matrix of content dependency and to "dance in the kitchen instead," as you will surely do upon reading her informative personal story.

Her profound description of her relationship with her mother, for instance, in her kitchen demonstrated how “the learning among organisms is an ongoing practice of trying on language" and then "trying again with new language." She also shares her own messy but beautiful exploration of intercultural dynamics through her attempt to make Swedish meatballs now that she is living in Sweden.

In the chapter that, to me, captures the energy of this book, "giving what was taken" (no capital lettering, page 121-23), Nora continues, as in each chapter, to intertwine the threads of interdependence through the nurturing that emanates from her kitchen. She describes how this creates mutual learning, which, to her, is "life." This occurs through "graciousness" that is not for show: "...it is how life offers life towards life." In other words, if someone takes what you make for them to eat, made with your hands, and accepts your care and love, "this is an intimate moment of contact and communication." This is reciprocal interdependence and nourishment. It is nature's mitigating gift of improvisation, occurring in all aspects and contexts of our world.

When this occurs, possibilities expand far beyond what one can imagine. In ecological thinking, this change makes a difference. Sustaining and expanding these differences is a new level of change: from one interaction to the infinite interactions of our world, we can and should keep making differences. Nora explains that perceiving change is like zooming in and out, allowing us to simultaneously see the immediate and wider contexts at the same time. This is systems thinking at its best, whether in the kitchen or elsewhere: what is relevant in the moment combines more than ingredients, including the full gamut of social, seasonal, cultural, and time-dependent factors. Any system torn from its contextual relationships creates polarities. It is a process “entangled in many more processes of being alive than just speaking.” Any and all fragmentation violates life.

Another message she focuses on is the danger of our species becoming like vultures, getting used to feeding off unhealthy, soiled food. This certainty and generalization about what is good for us flattens our complexity, which, when tolerated, creates a false sense of respect. Whereas this form of reductionism may be attractive, it is an addiction going up the wrong road. She advocates that we should acquire the need to be among, to mingle; “kneading together may be nth order change,” or infinite differences. Without this, competition and conflict become part of that addiction and can be an escalating horror.

With mutual learning and respect for interdependency, Nora prompts us with "My story can change your story if we allow it to happen." Then we can cherish what she calls “quickening in non-linear living," which is “Aphanipoisis,” a word that she coined, meaning “the coalescing of unseen processes that make vitality." The opposite of being "among" this vitality is isolation.

Ecological logic welcomes movement and interdependency. Rhythms and patterning are a way of being life. This process and patterning encourages progressive changes to our ecological benefit. In this wonderful book, Nora demonstrates, through narratives of warmth and love around the kitchen table, the need for more storytelling and mutual learning to help us tend to the needs of others and our world, and to respect these part-to-whole relationships.

I highly recommend this delightful, delicious book, with over 50 pieces of art and profound stories interspersed with genuine, incredible poems that relate to her intertwining narrative descriptions and invite you to savor it. item.title: An Engineering Strategy for Testing Self-Improvement Plans
item.description:
Self-Help

An Engineering Strategy for Testing Self-Improvement Plans

Your emotional life will benefit from this type of systematic thinking.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Backtesting uses past data to verify if a new plan fixes a repeated problem.
  • Stress-testing plans against past events may risk ignoring new, unforeseen variables.
  • Backtesting works for habits and stress by revealing early triggers and off-ramps.
Source: AI Generated Image

Backtesting is a technique used to test a new system based on whether it would have done what you needed it to do in a past situation, where you already have existing data of exactly what happened and the specific stress the system would’ve needed to withstand.

Let’s first explore a business example and then see how the principles translate to personal situations.

Business case: You run a website, and your server got overloaded during a promotion. You upgrade and then simulate the exact conditions that occurred before to see if the new setup could handle the prior conditions.

The main negative of backtesting is that it can cause you to "overfit" your plans to past scenarios but fail to anticipate new ones. For instance, you plan for how your website could withstand a sudden influx of real users but not an army of bots.

Or, in a personal context, you design a system for how to not let your exercise routine be overly disrupted when your child is sick, but the plan doesn't account for if you're sick.

The positive of backtesting is that it sets a floor. If your new system couldn't handle the exact situation you already encountered, then you know that you didn’t solve your problem yet.

Real World Situations Where Backtesting Could Be Useful

The following are situations that tend to recur, where you might want to better prevent the issue or improve your response. The examples start practical and then extend into more emotional and interpersonal realms.

  • You ran out of something and getting more in a hurry was highly inconvenient.
  • You lock yourself out.
  • You keep paying for a subscription you haven't used in over a year.
  • You left something you needed for school at a friend's house.
  • You arrived at the pharmacy, asked for your prescription, and they had no record of it.
  • Under stress, you became absorbed or distracted and did something dangerous, or that created more stress (like you mishandled a weight at the gym or got distracted writing an email on your phone between sets and someone complained you were on the machine too long).
  • In the process of moving, you miss a bill that goes to collections and harms your credit score.
  • You were impatient with your children because you were stressed. You regretted it.
  • You let a health concern (e.g., a skin or bowel-habit change) go longer than you should have without getting help.
  • You were asked an intrusive question and didn’t like how you handled it.
  • You realized after the fact a situation was probably negotiable, but you didn’t think to negotiate.

If you’ve experienced a problem multiple times, then you have multiple past scenarios you can backtest your new plans against.

Use AI to Help You Generate Alternative Scenarios

LLMs can be great at “adversarial review” of plans. To stress test your self-improvement plan, you can ask them, “What situations doesn't my plan handle well?”

Sometimes you’ll need to break the AI out of tunnel vision, in which it considers one angle too intensively but completely overlooks others.

Why Backtest?

Backtesting encourages you to take a systematic approach to problem-solving and self-improvement.

Since it’s specific and measurable, it can especially help if you’re prone to diffuse worry and/or avoid practical problem-solving.

Don’t Limit Yourself to Practicalities

As hinted at in the examples, you can use this approach for emotion regulation and interpersonal topics, not just practicalities like organization and routines.

Worked Example

Say you don't want to become impatient with your children when you’re stressed. Your plan would need to include how you were going to recognize you’re in an emotional state in which this could occur, what constraints might be present or absent, what resources might be available or not available, and where different “off-ramps” are possible (or "on-ramps" in different situations).

If you’re getting your kids in the car to drop them off at school, your strategy might be different than if it’s the beginning of a Saturday and you’re going to be with them all day.

In the school drop-off scenario, you might think about the earliest sign of stress you could recognize, like looking at the clock and thinking “we’re late” or waking up worrying about a “to-do” that’s on your list for that day.

If you wake up worried, your off-ramp might be that you deliberately compartmentalize the adult problem till right after the school drop-off, and in the meantime use some self-talk to remind yourself that you can handle stressful things.

Your backtest might allow you to realize there was nothing to be gained from ruminating about your adult problem during the get-ready-for-school routine, and that putting off thinking about it for under an hour was achievable for you.

You might consider whether specific caring routines could automate away some potential for irritability to sneak in, like you always give your child a quick kiss when you’re helping them put their shoes on.

Don’t Reserve Backtesting for Major Problems

Backtesting can be a useful strategy for problems big and small, and practicing using it for more minor scenarios (especially if they have emotional or interpersonal elements) can help you gain experience with the technique that benefits you for trickier ones.

item.title: Can Good Come from Adversity?
item.description:
Disaster Psychology

Can Good Come from Adversity?

We can learn important lessons from four disasters that changed the world.

Posted September 18, 2026

Key points
  • Disasters are increasing in intensity and frequency.
  • If society doesn't learn from previous disasters, it's bound to repeat them.
  • Four disasters changed the world, and in doing so, taught us how to prepare for the next.
Source: fernandozhiminaicela/ Pixabay

It seems both mainstream, cable, and even social media are consumed with discussions of past disasters (9/11, floods, COVID-19) or speculations on impending disasters (AI gone rogue). The United Nations has confirmed that disasters are increasing in frequency and intensity.

Harvard professor George Santayana once wrote, “Progress, far from consisting in change, depends on retentiveness … and when experience is not retained, infancy is perpetual. Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.”

This is a valuable warning. But more valuable yet is the admonition of Alvin Toffler, who said, “If we do not learn from history, we shall be compelled to relive it. True. But if we do not change the future, we shall be compelled to endure it. And that could be worse.”

Disasters are devastating, but perhaps we can learn valuable lessons from them to help shape the future. This post looks at four modern disasters that changed the world and the lessons we can take from them that might prepare us for the future. Failure to do so could be unimaginable.

Tokyo Sarin Gas Attack

On March 20, 1995, members of Aum Shinrikyo punctured bags of sarin. Sarin is a potentially fatal nerve agent that causes acute cholinergic reactions, especially feelings of suffocation. The release killed 12 people and caused more than 5,000 to seek medical care, causing chaos across the subway system and overwhelming hospitals with about 1,000 victims physically exposed and over 4,000 people who feared they had been exposed.

The disaster revealed two phenomena: psychological contagion and the psychological iceberg effect. Psychological contagion refers to the spread of fear, general distress, and even physical reactions that mimic actual exposure to the pathogen, but absent any actual exposure. The psychological iceberg effect refers to the fact that psychological casualties can (and almost always do) vastly outnumber physical casualties in the wake of disasters by a ratio of 50:1 or more. This is especially true in the case of radiation, chemical, and biological agents.

The disaster taught two powerful lessons: 1) the importance of ongoing crisis communications to the affected community to combat uncertainty and fear, and 2) the importance of both physical and psychological triage to direct survivors to the most efficient and effective resources. Finally, crisis communications should follow the 3-T guidance: truthful, transparent, timely.

Hurricane Katrina

Hurricane Katrina was referred to as an example of catastrophic leadership failure. Katrina made landfall on August 29, 2005, as a Category 3 hurricane. It devastated the Gulf Coast of the United States—especially New Orleans—costing 1800 lives and displacing over 100,000 people.

Even though evacuation was recommended by federal weather authorities, the mayor delayed until evacuation was no longer an option. There was no clear-cut evacuation mechanism for over 100,000 people who did not have cars. State authorities delayed allowing access to external logistical and medical resources for fear of adverse legal ramifications. Federal authorities underestimated the severity of the impact. Temporary housing was abandoned for fear of toxicity, potentially leaving thousands homeless.

Perhaps the greatest lesson learned from Katrina was that “he who hesitates is lost.” Surely, the moment of absolute certainty never arrives. The only failure in crisis leadership is the failure to lead. Finally, paralysis by analysis or out of fear can be deadly.

September 11, 2001 (9/11)

On September 11, 2001, Al‑Qaeda terrorists, in a coordinated effort, hijacked four jet passenger planes and crashed them into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. It goes without saying that those attacks reshaped the entire world for the following 25 years and will continue to do so. Over 3,000 people were killed as a direct result of the attacks, but many more have died as indirect victims through illness and retaliatory warfare. According to a September 10, 2026 report on CBS News, the Mt. Sinai medical system continues to treat over 25,000 first responders for mental health issues.

Perhaps the greatest lessons from 9/11 were the destruction of a national sense of invulnerability (we seemed to forget the previous attempt to destroy the World Trade Center on February 26, 1996) and how enduring and widespread traumatic stress, depression, and grief can be in the wake of disaster.

The COVID-19 Pandemic

The COVID‑19 pandemic was a global infectious‑disease disaster caused by the SARS‑CoV‑2 virus, beginning in late 2019. It disrupted every aspect of daily life worldwide—health systems, economies, communities, and even interpersonal social functioning. There were over 775,000,000 confirmed cases with over 7,000,000 confirmed deaths.

Lessons learned from COVID-19 were numerous. Psychologically, COVID was a disaster of uncertainty. Uncertainty was revealed to be the foundation for the subsequent psychological pandemic of anxiety and depression. Reviews found the prevalence of anxiety rose from 8 to 23 percent and depression rose from 5 to 25 percent (Hou et al., 2025). COVID-19 exposed systemic weaknesses in global governance, international cooperation, national policy formation, and crisis leadership. COVID-19 was a textbook case of failure in all of Everly’s five factors of effective crisis leadership (Everly & Athey, 2023). Moral injury, once thought to be primarily related to combat, became epidemic amongst healthcare workers. Perhaps the three greatest mistakes made during the pandemic were failed crisis communications, allowing persistent social isolation to destroy social infrastructures, and politicizing the pandemic.

As the Phoenix arises from disaster stronger than before, learning from the adversity and mistakes made in disaster, we too can arise stronger than before. The failure to learn from our mistakes, however, condemns us to repeat them.
